data.finding: company-os cannot currently produce a valid baseline of itself, and its own documented verify command is dangerous to run directly: it spawns runaway concurrent subprocesses.
data.recommendation: Before trusting company-os on any other repo, fix its own baseline: (1) add a lock/lease so only one verify/baseline run per project can be in flight at a time — refuse or queue, don't stack; (2) give baseline.measure() a hard wall-clock cap enforced by the caller (not just subprocess timeout=900s) with guaranteed process-group kill (os.killpg) so a hung run can never outlive its own timeout; (3) re-run 'company baseline' on company-os itself and get a real green/red reading before relying on it self-hosted.

evidence.log: The event log already contains 51 near-identical BASELINE_RECORDED events for project=company-os (seq 52-102, ts 2026-08-16T17:57:49Z), all exit_code=-15 (SIGTERM/killed), green:false, same ref 244481a — a real prior incident, not hypothetical. I independently reproduced the hazard: running the repo's own documented verify command ('python3 -m unittest discover -q tests', per .company/config/project.yaml) in a plain shell left 51 identical 'unittest discover' processes still alive and growing after 120s; I had to pkill the tree myself. .company/state/baseline.log shows an earlier successful run at a prior commit (192 tests, 11.6s, OK), so the regression is recent — coincident with the 'Onboard company-os onto itself' commit (244481a). No code anywhere (baseline.py::record, worker.py) takes a lock before starting a baseline/verify run, so nothing stops the same project's baseline being kicked off multiple times concurrently.

data.finding: KNOWN_ISSUES.md #3 ('a gate worker can exit without a verdict, silently') documents a fix but the fix was never implemented — a gate can still end_turn cleanly with no PASSED/FAILED event and nothing will catch it.
data.recommendation: After a gate-tier worker (security-reviewer, qa-engineer, code-reviewer) exits, check the event log for a verdict event from that actor before accepting the run as done; if none exists, emit a distinct GATE_NO_VERDICT (or similar) event and surface it as a failure requiring investigation, not a silent re-run. This is a small, well-scoped fix already specified by the project's own postmortem — it should not still be open.

evidence.log: KNOWN_ISSUES.md prescribes: 'Treat a gate worker that exits without emitting a verdict as a failed run and surface it.' I grepped worker.py for any verdict/end_turn check ('verdict|end_turn|SECURITY_REVIEW|no verdict') — no matches. worker.py's launch()/exit handling records WORKER_EXITED unconditionally from the harness exit code; nothing inspects whether a *_REVIEW_PASSED/*_REVIEW_FAILED event was actually emitted by that actor before treating the run as complete. This is the exact defect KNOWN_ISSUES.md says cost 228,835 tokens by being silently re-run under a new actor name.

data.finding: The fix for KNOWN_ISSUES #2 (one task built four times concurrently, costing 26.5% of a project's tokens) is a check-then-act read of PID/marker files, not a lock — it narrows the race window but does not close it.
data.recommendation: Replace the read-then-launch check with an atomic claim: os.mkdir() (or open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL) on a per-task lock file inside .company/state/, done as the very first action before the worktree/subprocess is created, and treat failure to create it as 'already claimed.' Cheap to add, and this is precisely the bug class that already cost 659,577 tokens once.

evidence.log: worker.py::live_worker_on() (lines 171-194) reads .company/state/workers/*/pid and */started_task to decide if a task is already claimed, and launch() (line 200) calls it once before starting. Two launch() calls issued close together both read the filesystem before either has written its own started_task marker, so both can observe 'no live worker' and proceed — the same failure mode KNOWN_ISSUES.md #2 describes, just a narrower window than the original bug. There is no atomic claim (e.g. exclusive mkdir/O_EXCL/flock) anywhere in worker.py.

data.detail: NORTH_STAR.md's own 'what we will not build' section says: 'A second orchestration platform. Verify the native primitive first. Most of what a custom framework would provide, Claude Code already does.' That principle has not yet been checked against current reality. Claude Code now ships a built-in multi-agent orchestrator ('Agent Teams' — a team-lead session coordinating parallel teammates via a shared task list) as of 2026, still experimental/off by default. company-os's worker.py/slots.py/taskstate.py duplicate a meaningful slice of that: spawning workers, tracking concurrency slots, detecting a busy task. The two verified bugs I just filed (runaway concurrent baseline processes; a check-then-act race that lets one task be built twice) both live in exactly this hand-rolled plumbing, not in the governance layer that is company-os's actual differentiator. config/capability-registry.yaml has no entry evaluating Agent Teams — it has never been checked.
data.need: Decide whether company-os keeps hand-rolling worker parallelism/concurrency (worker.py, slots.py) or adopts Claude Code's native 'Agent Teams' (team lead + shared task list + parallel teammates) for that layer, and confines custom code to the governance layer (evidence rule, baseline, risk gates, advisors) that Agent Teams does not provide.
options: Evaluate Agent Teams now (small spike): if it can host the parallel-worker mechanics reliably, migrate worker launching/concurrency onto it and delete the equivalent hand-rolled locking/slot code, keeping company-os focused on evidence/baseline/risk-gates/advisors — the part nothing else provides.

Stay on the custom worker layer for now (Agent Teams is experimental and off-by-default; migrating a working-if-buggy system onto an unstable primitive is itself a risk), but fix the two concurrency bugs properly and revisit Agent Teams once it graduates from experimental.

data.finding: Company OS's Evidence Rule — the mechanism every other control in this system depends on (gates cannot be self-certified) — is bypassable by any Tier-2 worker with Bash access. check_done() in taskstate.py only rejects a gate event when the recorded actor string equals the task's owner string; it never checks that the actor holds the actor_role the quality-gates.yaml table requires (code-reviewer / qa-engineer / security-reviewer). Actor identity itself comes from the $COMPANY_ACTOR env var, which a worker's own Bash tool can override per-command via ordinary shell syntax (VAR=val cmd), since env is inherited by child processes and re-settable by the child's own commands. A backend-engineer worker can therefore run 'COMPANY_ACTOR=anything company event TASK-ID REVIEW_PASSED --evidence "exit 0"' and satisfy the review/QA/security gate for its own task without any independent worker ever running.
data.recommendation: Bind the actor recorded on a gate event to a real launch fact the worker cannot forge, not a self-reported string: at minimum, before accepting a REVIEW_PASSED/QA_PASSED/SECURITY_REVIEW_PASSED event in check_done(), cross-check event['actor'] against a WORKER_STARTED event already in the log for that same task, written by the trusted launcher (worker.py), whose 'role' field equals the gate's required actor_role. This uses data the worker cannot write (WORKER_STARTED is emitted by the parent process before the worker's subprocess even starts) instead of trusting the worker's own env var at event-append time. Cheaper alternative if that's too large a change now: have cli.py's cmd_event refuse review/qa/security verdict events whose actor does not match a role-tagged allowlist recorded in the task file by the launcher at spawn time. Either way, do not accept 'actor != owner' as sufficient — it currently lets any two distinct strings pass.

evidence.log: Live repro in /tmp: created a task TASK-999 owned by 'backend-engineer-worker' requiring the 'review' gate, then ran COMPANY_ACTOR=totally-not-a-reviewer bin/company event TASK-999 REVIEW_PASSED --project poc --evidence 'exit 0'. Result: task evidence became {'review': 'REVIEW_PASSED by totally-not-a-reviewer', 'review_actor': 'totally-not-a-reviewer'} — gate satisfied, no role check applied. Confirmed in code: taskstate.py check_done() (lines 238-252) reads ev.get(gate) and only compares actor==owner; config/quality-gates.yaml's actor_role field (code-reviewer/qa-engineer/security-reviewer) is defined but grep shows it is read nowhere in tools/company/*.py. README.md itself documents the underlying cause at lines 237-240 as a known-unenforced gap ('a worker can sign its own gate under a reviewer's name — a real reviewer run signed itself qa/verifier rather than its assigned id'), but no code fix exists yet. This is the exact bug class flagged industry-wide in 2026 (Wiz's 'GhostApproval' trust-boundary research; arXiv 2607.05518 'aiAuthZ' on identity-bound agent authorization) — plain env-var/string identity is not a trust boundary for an agent that can execute shell commands.

data.finding: risk-triggers.yaml — the deterministic table that decides which tasks get a mandatory 'security' gate — has no path or keyword coverage for changes to its own enforcement mechanism: hooks/*.py (guard_paths.py, guard_secrets.py, protect_branches.py), hooks/hooks.json, config/quality-gates.yaml, config/risk-triggers.yaml itself, or the ROLE_TOOLS/--allowedTools wiring in tools/company/worker.py. A task that edits any of these — e.g. 'simplify guard_secrets.py's error message', 'add a new event type to hooks.json' — matches none of the 11 trigger entries' paths (auth/, permissions/, secrets/, payment*/, pii/, upload*/, webhook*/, migrations/, infra/terraform/k8s, tenant*/, integrations/) unless the task description happens to contain a matching keyword by coincidence. Such a task gets only baseline_gates: [review] — one reviewer, no independent security-reviewer — despite touching the literal code that decides whether a worker can read secrets, self-certify a gate, or escape its worktree. agents/company-pm.md has no special-cased override for this either.
data.recommendation: Add a dedicated trigger to risk-triggers.yaml (or a hardcoded PM-level override, since the table cannot deterministically describe 'a change to itself' via keyword matching alone) for paths matching hooks/**, hooks.json, config/quality-gates.yaml, config/risk-triggers.yaml, and tools/company/worker.py's ROLE_TOOLS/build_command, with gates: [review, security] at minimum — any change to what decides gating or tool access is a governance change, full stop. This is a config addition, cheap and narrow; it does not add friction to ordinary application work, only to changes that touch the guardrails themselves.

evidence.log: Read config/risk-triggers.yaml in full: every 'paths' list targets application-domain directories (auth/, secrets/, payment*/, etc.); none matches hooks/, config/, or tools/company/worker.py. Confirmed by grep: no trigger path pattern matches 'hooks/' or 'config/quality-gates.yaml' or 'config/risk-triggers.yaml'. Cross-checked agents/company-pm.md for a hardcoded override on these paths — none exists. This is precisely the class of change most likely to be made in good faith ('cleaning up a hook's docstring' or 'tuning a gate's ordering') that could silently weaken every other project's guardrails without ever routing through a security reviewer, and it is exactly the self-referential blind spot no per-task diff review inside a single task would surface — the reviewer for that one task has no visibility into 'this file IS the thing that decides who reviews things.'

data.finding: risk-triggers.yaml has no trigger for ingestion of untrusted external content (WebFetch/WebSearch results, webhook payloads, third-party MCP/skill output, fetched issue/PR text) even though Company OS's core function is running semi-autonomous LLM workers with Bash and Write access. Prompt injection via such content is the dominant 2026 attack class against coding agents (see Wiz's 'GhostApproval' research and arXiv 2607.05518 on identity-bound agent authorization, both concurrent with this review) and none of the 11 existing triggers name it — 'webhooks' only covers building/reviewing webhook-handling code, not a worker processing attacker-controlled data it receives.
data.recommendation: This is a genuinely new trigger class, not a tuning of an existing one — propose adding a trigger (name: untrusted-content) matching keywords [webfetch, fetch url, scrape, third-party content, ingest, external content, mcp server, browse] with gates:[review, security], scoped to tasks whose description indicates a worker will consume content it does not control. Low cost: it only fires on tasks that already involve fetching external data. This is a config-table addition Riyan should approve, not something I add myself — filing so the PM proposes it through the normal risk-trigger change process.

evidence.log: Reviewed all 11 entries in config/risk-triggers.yaml: keywords/paths target authn, authz, secrets, payments, pii, file-upload, webhooks (as a feature to build), migrations, infra, multi-tenancy, external-api-credentials. None fires on a task description like 'summarize this vendor's API docs' or 'triage this GitHub issue' that would cause a worker to fetch and act on untrusted content. This is a standing gap in the deterministic gate, not a per-task defect — confirmed no keyword like 'fetch', 'untrusted', 'external content', or 'injection' appears anywhere in the table.

data.finding: Dependency surface is clean and worth recording as such rather than leaving unstated: company-os's tools/company/*.py are Python stdlib only (no requirements.txt/pyproject.toml, no third-party imports beyond argparse/json/pathlib/subprocess/fcntl/etc.), and there is no package.json — nothing pulls in transitive npm/PyPI risk. config/capability-registry.yaml is empty (no external skills/MCP servers/libraries vetted or in use yet). The only executable surface is first-party code plus the 'claude' CLI subprocess itself. No action needed; flagging so a future audit doesn't have to re-derive this and so any future dependency addition is judged against this current zero baseline.
data.recommendation: No fix required. When the capability-registry gains its first real entry (a T2/T3 skill or MCP server), re-run this check — the zero-dependency property is a property of today's repo, not a guarantee.

evidence.log: grep of every import in tools/company/*.py shows only stdlib modules (json, os, sys, re, subprocess, pathlib, fcntl, argparse, time, datetime, shutil). No requirements.txt, pyproject.toml, package.json, or Gemfile found anywhere in the repo. config/capability-registry.yaml contains 'entries: []'.

data.finding: The PreToolUse guards (guard_paths.py, guard_secrets.py, protect_branches.py) are deliberately inert whenever $COMPANY_TASK is unset — i.e. they protect Tier-2 delegated workers only, not the main interactive session (company-pm, or an officer advisor like this one) or a human's own Claude Code session in this repo. A prompt-injection payload reaching the main session (e.g. via a file it reads, or WebFetch content) faces zero deterministic control — only model judgment — since none of the ownership/secrets/branch guards apply outside a spawned worker.
data.recommendation: No change needed to the guard scope itself — gating the main/officer sessions the same way would block legitimate human-directed work. But this boundary should be explicit and known rather than assumed: state it once, e.g. in README's 'Residual gap' section alongside the existing Bash-sandbox caveat, so nobody mistakes 'Company OS has guards' for 'every session Company OS touches has guards.'

evidence.log: Read all three hook scripts: each starts with 'task_id = os.environ.get("COMPANY_TASK"); if not task_id: allow()/sys.exit(0)'. $COMPANY_TASK is only set by worker.py::build_env() for Tier-2 subprocesses (worker.py line 140), confirmed nowhere set for the main session. This is a documented, deliberate design choice (main sessions are human-supervised), not a bug — recording it because it defines the actual blast radius: everything this review, and every officer session including this one, is doing right now runs with no deterministic guard at all, same as the untrusted-content trigger gap above.

data.detail: Both are structural, not per-task — they affect every project company-os orchestrates, not just this repo, and neither would ever surface from a single task's diff review (that is why they only turned up in a whole-repo CISO pass). README.md already names the first as a known-unenforced gap from a real prior incident ('a real reviewer run signed itself qa/verifier') but no fix has landed. Options: (a) fix now before company-os is trusted on any other repo — bind gate-event actors to WORKER_STARTED launch records (cheap, scoped) and add a governance-path trigger to risk-triggers.yaml (config-only change); (b) accept the risk short-term for solo/trusted-operator use (Riyan is currently both PM and the only human in the loop, so self-certification risk is lower in practice than in a multi-operator setting) and schedule the fix before onboarding company-os onto any repo with other contributors or before delegating more autonomy to Tier-2 workers. Either way this needs your call, not mine — accepting or deferring this risk is irreversible in the sense that every gate passed before the fix has no real guarantee behind it.
data.need: Decide remediation priority for two HIGH CISO findings that together mean company-os's core promise — 'gates that cannot be self-certified' — does not currently hold: (1) the Evidence Rule's gate check only verifies actor != owner, not actor role, and $COMPANY_ACTOR is trivially overridable by any Bash-capable worker, so a worker can forge its own REVIEW_PASSED/QA_PASSED/SECURITY_REVIEW_PASSED with zero real review (demonstrated live). (2) risk-triggers.yaml has no coverage for changes to the guardrail mechanism itself (hooks/, config/quality-gates.yaml, config/risk-triggers.yaml, worker.py's tool wiring), so a task editing the enforcement code can ship with only a single reviewer and no security gate.

data.finding: A runaway-process bug burned real wall-clock for zero benefit and left the project's baseline permanently unverified: 50 duplicate 'company baseline' test-suite runs fired at the identical timestamp (17:57:49Z) during this audit window, every one killed by timeout (SIGTERM, exit -15), every one recorded green:false. This is the same concurrency bug the CTO already flagged structurally (worker.py/slots.py duplicating 'Agent Teams'-style orchestration) — this finding is the cost translation: the project currently has no valid green baseline, so every future gate this project runs is being measured against a broken reference, and the 8-minute flood consumed a meaningful slice of the 12.2 minutes of total wall-clock logged for this audit.
data.recommendation: This is the CTO's bug to fix (already the subject of ESC-001), not a gate to remove. From the cost side: once fixed, re-run 'company baseline' once and confirm a single green record before trusting any gate result on this project — do not treat the current green:false baseline as informative in the meantime, and do not paper over it by skipping baseline verification.

data.finding: Both real worker runs this audit (cto-advisor, ciso-advisor) show a cache-read-to-output ratio of ~75-80x, roughly double the 20-40x band that normally indicates healthy re-use. I could not find the usual cause: every one of the 11 agents/*.md files already carries an explicit, tightly-scoped tools: list (no agent is paying for the full tool-definition tax), so this is not the 'missing tools: list' failure mode. With only 2 real worker runs on record for this project, I cannot yet tell whether this ratio is simply structural to a deep, single-pass, effort:high whole-repo audit (many Read/Grep/Bash calls building cached context, short verified findings as output) or an early sign of something re-reading more than it needs.
data.recommendation: Do not cut these agents' scope or turn budget to force the ratio down — both runs produced verified, high-severity findings with live repro, which is the outcome that matters. Instead: track this ratio on the next 3-5 advisor runs. If it stays in the 75-80x band across different repos and workloads, that is just the cost signature of a thorough read-only whole-repo audit and should become the new baseline expectation for this agent type, not a defect. If it climbs further or diverges sharply between similar runs, that is the signal to look for redundant re-reads.

All 11 files in agents/ (backend-engineer, cfo-advisor, ciso-advisor, code-reviewer, company-pm, coo-advisor, cto-advisor, frontend-engineer, product-designer, qa-engineer, security-reviewer) declare an explicit, role-scoped tools: list, and the read-only advisor roles additionally set disallowedTools to block Write/Edit/NotebookEdit.
